<reason>Side B (PRO) won a closely fought, high-quality debate. B kept the dispute anchored to the motion as written—the word "solely"—and maintained a clean boundary between conduct-based operational reasons (fraud, chargebacks, provenance) and association-based exclusion. A's central move was to rebrand reputational fear as "counterparty risk" measurable in dollars; B's response that a price tag on public hostility cannot settle the justification, and that A's rule lets threatened disapproval function as an indirect veto, was the more principled and less evasive position. B answered A's pressure questions honestly (no bailout promised, inability to settle is an independent operational reason, enforceable version requires stated reasons and review), while A's A2 answer conceded that exclusion is justified even with perfect age-gating and no likely financial loss—pure brand preference—which B's closing weaponized effectively as the decisive concession. A's "who spends the asset" property framing was rhetorically strong and coherent, but it rested on contested premises B had already challenged, and A's Rebuttal 2 was clipped for exceeding the word limit, an execution cost. Both sides used proper A1/A2 format and avoided fake sourcing. B made the debate easier to decide by forcing A to defend the hardest version of its own case and then showing exactly what that defense costs.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's pressure question Q2 ("why must the party carrying the liability yield?") forced Side B to choose between a bailout and toothless moral suasion; B's A1/A2 answers conceded no bailout but reframed the question as who gets power from disapproval, while A's own A2 concession—that exclusion stands even with no evidence of financial loss, as brand "stewardship"—gave B the decisive foothold it exploited in closing.</best_rebuttal>
